extracted.intended_audience: press freedom researchers, journalists, human-rights defenders, RSF staff and index users
extracted.subtask_description: Methodology for compiling and scoring the RSF World Press Freedom Index: definition of press freedom, questionnaire-based qualitative assessment, quantitative tally of abuses, five contextual indicators, safety/abuse scoring function, and presentation/thresholds. Intended to guide consistent scoring of 180 countries and territories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of press freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: “Press freedom is defined as the ability of journalists as individuals and collectives to select, produce, and disseminate news in the public interest independent of political, economic, legal, and social interference and in the absence of threats to their physical and mental safety.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This working definition underpins the choice of indicators and questions: emphasis on independence from political/economic/legal/social interference and absence of threats to physical and mental safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Index timeframe and update rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The Index is a snapshot of the situation during the calendar year (January–December) prior to publication, but is updated if the press freedom situation changes dramatically between the end of the year assessed and publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Updates are applied for major events such as war, coup d'état, major attacks on journalists, or sudden extreme repressive policy. The Index should reflect the situation at time of publication where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall score composition and scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Each country/territory receives a score ranging from 0 to 100 (100 = highest level of press freedom). The score is calculated on the basis of two components: a quantitative tally of abuses against media and journalists, and a qualitative analysis based on responses to an RSF questionnaire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two-component approach balances objective incident tallying with contextual expert judgement from press freedom specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative analysis via questionnaire
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative analysis is based on responses from press freedom specialists (including journalists, researchers, academics and human-rights defenders) to an RSF questionnaire available in 24 languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questionnaire languages listed: Arabic, Bulgarian, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, Czech, English, German, Persian, French, Greek, Hindi, Hungarian, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Mongolian, Polish, Portuguese, Romanian, Russian, Spanish, Turkish, Ukrainian. Responses feed the five contextual indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five contextual indicators (equal weighting)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Index evaluates each country using five contextual indicators: political context, legal framework, economic context, sociocultural context and safety. A subsidiary score (0–100) is calculated for each indicator and all five contribute equally to the global score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within each indicator, all questions and subquestions have equal weight. The equal-weight design is fundamental to score aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political context indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Political context (33 questions and subquestions) aims to evaluate: the degree of support and respect for media autonomy vis-à-vis political pressure; the level of acceptance of a variety of journalistic approaches (including politically aligned and independent approaches); and support for media in holding politicians and government to account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contains 33 questions/subquestions; results form one equally-weighted subsidiary score contributing to the global score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal framework indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal framework (25 questions and subquestions) aims to evaluate: freedom to work without censorship or judicial sanctions/excessive restrictions on freedom of expression; ability to access information without discrimination and to protect sources; and presence/absence of impunity for those responsible for acts of violence against journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contains 25 questions/subquestions; assesses statutory and judicial aspects that affect journalists' ability to operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic context indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic context (25 questions and subquestions) aims to evaluate: economic constraints linked to governmental policies (difficulty creating media outlets, favouritism in state subsidies, corruption); constraints linked to non-state actors (advertisers, commercial partners); and constraints from media owners promoting/defending business interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contains 25 questions/subquestions; focuses on market and ownership pressures that impair editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociocultural context indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Sociocultural context (22 questions and subquestions) aims to evaluate: social constraints from denigration/attacks on the press based on gender, class, ethnicity, religion; and cultural constraints such as pressure not to question powerful institutions or to avoid covering sensitive issues because of prevailing culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contains 22 questions/subquestions; captures social norms and prejudice-driven pressures affecting journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety indicator (questions + abuses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Safety comprises 12 questions/subquestions (accounting for two-thirds of the safety score) evaluating risks to journalists (bodily harm, psychological/emotional distress, professional harm). One-third of the safety score comes from a separate abuses score derived from RSF’s tally of abuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safety is explicitly defined to include bodily harm (murder, violence, arrest, detention, enforced disappearance, abduction), psychological harms (intimidation, coercion, harassment, surveillance, doxing, smears), and professional harms (job loss, equipment confiscation, ransacking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuses score calculation method
rubrics_metrics.description: The abuses score is calculated from RSF’s tally of abuses by means of a function where x is the weighted sum of abuses in a country in the calendar year prior to the Index relative to the decimal logarithm of the population size; K is a coefficient set to 0.15 to create a score distribution from 0 to 100.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral properties: when no abuse is registered the abuse score = 100; as the number of abuses increases, the score declines and tends toward 0. The population-normalized weighted sum (x) controls for country size. K=0.15 is used as a mathematical device to scale results to 0–100.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse severity hierarchy and coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Different kinds of abuses are assigned coefficients (k_i) to establish seriousness levels: murder (100); abduction (50); disappearance (50); detention coefficients vary by length (from 25 for <1 year up to 50 for >10 years); media ransacked/destroyed/closed/suspended (1). House arrest is counted as detention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A full coefficient table is provided; detention coefficients decrease stepwise by year bands (e.g., detention <1 year = 25; 1–2 years = 27.5; ... >10 years = 50). These coefficients weight the x_i counts when computing the abuses weighted sum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse categories counted
rubrics_metrics.description: Abuses counted include murders, abductions, disappearances, detention (with duration bands), and attacks on media outlets (ransacking, destruction, closure, suspension), among other abuses against journalists and media in connection with their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RSF staff constantly gather these incidents worldwide and update the press freedom barometer; specifics of categorization and counting feed the abuses weighted sum used in the abuses score function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population data sources and exceptions for normalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Population size (used to normalize the abuses tally) is taken from World Bank figures by default, with specified exceptions: Taiwan (local Statistical Bureau), Cyprus (Eurostat), Northern Cyprus (World Bank total minus Eurostat EU-member part), Montserrat (local government). The population figures used are the most recent available (e.g., 2021 for the 2023 Index, with exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using standardized population sources ensures comparability; exceptions are explicitly documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data gathering and updating (press freedom barometer)
rubrics_metrics.description: RSF staff constantly gather information globally about abuses against journalists; information about hostages, imprisoned, killed or missing journalists is updated daily on RSF’s press freedom barometer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Daily updates to the barometer feed the abuses tally and allow post-year adjustments when dramatic events occur between the assessed year and publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press freedom map classification thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: The press freedom map classifies countries by score ranges: [85–100] = good (green); [70–85[ = satisfactory (yellow); [55–70[ = problematic (light orange); [40–55[ = difficult (dark orange); [0–40[ = very serious (dark red).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These thresholds convert numeric scores into categorical labels for easy comparative visualisation on the map.
